title: Joseph of Cupertino (18 September)
hook: a slow student whose prayer was so intense that stories say he floated, patron of exam takers

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cornelius and Cyprian, a pope and a bishop who kept writing through their disagreements. Your line was friends who disagreed. What good thing did you say about someone? Day one thousand twenty-four.

Who gets turned away by a religious order? Joseph of Cupertino did, the story goes. A poor boy from a small town in southern Italy. Slow at his lessons. Clumsy. So lost in his own head that people teased him for wandering around with his mouth hanging open. He asked the friars to take him, and they sent him away. When he was finally let in, it was to work in the stable. Today, the saint students pray to before a test. Which has a joke folded inside it, because in the stories Joseph is bad at tests.
screen: `TURNED AWAY.` → `TAKEN IN, TO WORK THE STABLE.` → `THE SAINT OF TESTS.`

segments.voice: The stable worker kept praying, and over time the friars saw what was in him and let him study for the priesthood. Study did not go well. Here's the story Catholics tell. At one exam, the examiner opened the Gospel and asked him about a single passage, and it was the one text he knew well. He passed. At the next, the story goes, the first candidates answered so well that the bishop passed the rest of the group without questioning them, and Joseph was in that group. That's why students ask his prayers before exams. Then the strange part. Stories say that when Joseph prayed, especially at Mass, joy would seize him and he would rise off the ground. People came to see. Church authorities questioned him. His superiors, uneasy with the crowds, moved him to quiet friaries, out of sight. Catholics hold the floating stories in different ways. What they honor him for is his humility and his prayer. And underneath it all is a moment in Luke's Gospel. Jesus rejoices and thanks his Father for hiding these things from the wise and prudent. The Douay-Rheims finishes the line: "and hast revealed them to little ones." Joseph was a little one in that sense. Not clever, not polished, a little lost. But his prayer was so whole that, in the stories, it lifted him. So he's patron of exams not because he was smart, but because he wasn't, and he was carried through anyway. For Catholics who ask his prayers, a prayer before a test isn't a trick for better grades. It's someone small asking for help, the way Joseph did.
screen: `THE ONE TEXT HE KNEW.` · `STORIES SAY HE FLOATED.` · `HIDDEN FROM THE CLEVER.` · `CARRIED THROUGH.` · then, large: `SHOWN TO LITTLE ONES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a student. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is learning something hard right now. A child with homework, a teenager facing finals, a friend studying for a license, someone learning a new language at fifty. Think of the test in front of them, and the nerves. If you pray, you can ask Saint Joseph of Cupertino to pray for them, or pray for them in your own way. If you don't, just hold them in mind and wish them a steady head. The bell holds the time.
Little ones, Jesus's phrase for people like Joseph of Cupertino: the slow, poor student, taken in to work the stable, whose prayer stories say lifted him off the ground. Patron of exams.
Your line: patron of exams. Today, send a word of encouragement to someone facing a test of any kind. Keep it short, and don't ask how they think it'll go. Day one thousand twenty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the memory of Saint Joseph of Cupertino on 18 September, and students ask his prayers before exams; Franciscans honor him as one of their own.

original.note: Greek: an infant, a little one. in Luke 10:21 Jesus thanks the Father for revealing these things to them.

trapdoor: what you thought: the flying saint.
what it means: a slow, poor student, turned away and taken in at the stable, whose prayer carried him into the priesthood.
what a scholar hears: in Luke 10:21 the Douay-Rheims 'little ones' renders the Greek nēpioi, infants: Jesus thanks the Father for revealing things to them and not to the wise and prudent.

notes: Exam stories (asked the one passage he knew; the bishop passing the rest of the group) are given as 'the story Catholics tell'. Confirm.

Levitations are presented as 'stories say', and 'Catholics hold the floating stories in different ways'. 'Church authorities questioned him' refers to the Inquisition's examination. Confirm the framing.
Luke 10:21 is paraphrased (not quoted) because the exact Douay-Rheims wording wasn't certain.
Nickname 'Boccaperta' (open mouth) is described, not named. Confirm.
Practice mentions 'someone learning a new language at fifty' as an everyday example, not a claim.
howItsDone: confirm he is a Conventual Franciscan saint and that 'Franciscans honor him as one of their own' is fair.
